passage:
The one-star review arrived at nine: "Blouse fitting was off. Won't come back." Sarita, twenty-five, read it twice in her little tailoring shop in Jaipur and felt her stomach drop.
Himani, cutting fabric at the next table, winced. "Ouch."
Sarita took out the green notebook she kept in the drawer. "Before I decide this week was bad, let's count." She wrote: twelve orders delivered on time. Mrs. Rathore's thank-you note. The bride who sent a photo. Two customers who came back with friends. Then, in a separate column: one fitting complaint.
"So one miss out of fifteen," Himani said.
"A real miss. I'll call her and offer to fix it," Sarita said. "But it's one line, not the whole book."

qa.q: What did the one-star review say?
qa.a: "Blouse fitting was off. Won't come back."

qa.q: Why does Sarita reach for the green notebook right after the review?
qa.a: Sarita feels hurt by the review and knows one sharp review can feel like the whole week, so she wants to see the good things next to the bad before deciding how things are going.

qa.q: How does Sarita take the complaint seriously without overreacting?
qa.a: She calls it a real miss and plans to offer a fix, but writes it as one line beside twelve on-time orders and happy customers.

qa.q: How might the unhappy customer feel if Sarita calls to fix the blouse?
qa.a: The customer might feel heard and surprised, and perhaps less sure about never coming back. 🙂

grounding: It shows a grounded young woman counting her wins alongside a setback before judging how her week went.

"So? How was the appraisal?" Vijay asked, handing his wife a plate of poha.
"My manager said my reports are late sometimes," Preeti said.
"Oh no."
"Wait, I'm not done." She pulled out a folded paper. "I wrote down everything she said, good and bad, before I could forget the good parts. She said my client calls are the best on the team. She said the new joinees come to me for help. She said the Pune project went well because of me. And reports are late sometimes."
"That's three good, one bad."
"Exactly. On the bus I could feel the late-reports thing getting louder, so I read the list twice."
"And the reports?"
"Real. I'll block Friday mornings for them." She took a spoonful. "But I'm not calling it a bad appraisal."

qa.q: What did Preeti's manager say about the new joinees?
qa.a: That they come to her for help.

qa.q: Why did Preeti write down everything the manager said so quickly?
qa.a: She expected the criticism to get louder in her head and the praise to fade, so she wanted a fair record of both.

qa.q: How does Preeti respond to the one piece of criticism?
qa.a: She accepts it as real and plans to block Friday mornings for reports, without letting it turn the whole appraisal bad.

qa.q: How might Vijay's evening have gone if Preeti had come home talking only about late reports?
qa.a: Vijay might have spent the evening consoling her about a 'bad' appraisal that was actually mostly good.

grounding: It shows a grounded young woman giving praise the same weight as criticism before deciding how her appraisal went.

passage: Last March, after my under-14 team lost 4-0 in the district semi-final, I sat in the bus and decided I was a terrible coach. I'm Varun, I'd coached them for one season, and all I could see were the four goals. That night Nitin, my assistant, made me do something I now do after every tournament. We wrote two lists. Losses: the semi-final, one group match. Wins: eight matches, two shy kids who now speak up in the huddle, zero injuries, the whole squad still turning up at 6 a.m. in winter. The second list was longer, and just as true. I still went over what went wrong in the semi, because that mattered. But I stayed. We're in the final this year.

qa.q: What was the score in the district semi-final?
qa.a: The team lost 4-0.

qa.q: Why did Varun feel like a terrible coach on the bus ride back?
qa.a: Varun felt crushed because the painful loss filled Varun's view, so the four goals felt like the whole season even though much had gone well.

qa.q: What is useful about the two-list habit?
qa.a: It puts the wins on the page beside the losses, so decisions rest on the whole record, while still leaving room to study what went wrong.

qa.q: What would have changed for the players if Varun had quit after the semi-final?
qa.a: The shy kids who now speak up and the squad who turned up in winter would have lost a coach who helped them, and might not have reached this year's final.

grounding: It shows a young coach listing wins alongside losses before deciding how the season went.

passage:
Vice-principal's note, after the Class 6 parent feedback (Yogesh)
Swati, 24, is in her first year teaching English here. Thirty parents sent feedback forms this term. One was harsh: "Too soft, children talk in her class, she wastes time on stories."
Swati came to my office with that form in her hand, pale. But she didn't stop there. She asked for all thirty forms, sat at the side table and made two columns. Twenty-four forms praised her reading sessions. Several mentioned children who now read at home. Three asked for more homework. Then there was the harsh one.
She said, "I want to take the noise point seriously. But I'm not deciding I'm a bad teacher from one form."
Next: she'll try a quiet-reading signal in class, and I've asked her to share the parents' reading comments at the staff meeting.

qa.q: How many forms praised Swati's reading sessions?
qa.a: Twenty-four forms praised her reading sessions.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling when she first came to Yogesh's office, and how did that change?
qa.a: She was pale and shaken by the harsh form, but after counting all thirty she felt steadier and could take the noise point seriously without doubting herself as a teacher.

qa.q: Which choice helped Swati most, and why?
qa.a: Asking for all thirty forms and listing the praise next to the criticism, which stopped one harsh voice from deciding how she saw her whole term.

qa.q: How might the parents who wrote about children reading at home feel if the staff meeting hears their comments?
qa.a: Those parents would likely feel their feedback mattered, and pleased that the good change they noticed was taken as seriously as the complaint.

grounding: It shows a grounded young teacher deliberately counting praise alongside criticism and giving both weight before deciding how her term went.

passage:
Friday night
Launch day for the booking page. At 10 a.m. a client from the Pune office emailed our whole team: "Page is confusing. Who approved this?" My chest went tight and for an hour it was the only thing in my head.
Then I did the thing Joseph and I agreed on after last year's burnout: before deciding how a day went, write the wins next to the hits.
Wins: 412 bookings in the first day. Two emails from users saying it was easier than the old form. My lead said "clean work" in the stand-up. Mobile loading fixed after a week of fighting it. Joseph brought the good biscuits.
Hits: one angry client. One button label that honestly is confusing; I'll fix it Monday.
Looking at the page, it was a good day with one bad email in it. Not a bad day. I'm going to bed.
— Anjali

qa.q: How many bookings came in on the first day?
qa.a: 412 bookings in the first day.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling after the angry email, and what shows it?
qa.a: Anjali felt shaken and worried, with a tight chest and the email being the only thing on Anjali's mind for an hour.

qa.q: Which habit helped Anjali decide how the day really went?
qa.a: Writing the wins next to the hits, which let the bookings, the users' thanks and the lead's praise count as much as one angry email, while still fixing the confusing button.

qa.q: What would change if Anjali had judged the day only by the client's email?
qa.a: Anjali might have gone to bed thinking the launch failed, missed the real good news, and slid back towards the burnout of last year.

grounding: It shows a grounded person deliberately noting good events and counting wins alongside a setback before deciding how the day went.

passage: The gram sabha meeting in Karad ran late, and old Jadhav had shouted at Vishal in front of everyone: the new milk collection time was "useless". Walking home along the canal, Vishal felt the words sitting heavy on his chest. At home he didn't sulk. He took down the green notebook where he and Charu, the cooperative's accountant, logged every week. This week: thirty-eight families delivering on time, no spoiled cans, two new members, and a note from old Mrs Shinde thanking him for the early pickup. One angry farmer, with one fair point about the timing for those with far fields. "So, one problem, not a disaster," Charu said, reading over his shoulder. Vishal nodded and wrote: 'Visit Jadhav tomorrow, ask about a second pickup.'

qa.q: What did old Jadhav call the new milk collection time?
qa.a: He called it 'useless'.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling on the walk home, and how did he handle it?
qa.a: Vishal felt hurt, the words heavy on his chest, but chose to open the notebook and weigh the week's wins beside the complaint instead of sulking.

qa.q: Which part of Vishal's response was most useful, and why?
qa.a: Planning to visit Jadhav about a second pickup, because it took the complaint seriously after putting it in its true place among the week's successes.

qa.q: How might old Jadhav feel when Vishal visits the next day?
qa.a: Jadhav might feel heard and a little surprised that his angry point about far fields was taken seriously.

grounding: Shows a young organiser counting a week's wins alongside one loud complaint before deciding how things are and what to fix.

passage: On the last day of term in Manchester, Nadia carried the stack of student feedback slips to the staffroom. Last year she had flipped straight to the harsh ones and spent the summer chewing on them. This year she had a rule. She read every slip, then drew two columns on a sheet: 'working' and 'to fix'. Under 'working' went twenty-six slips: clear explanations, fair marking, the jokes. Under 'to fix' went four, three of them saying homework came back slowly. Jamal, marking beside her, glanced at the page. "That's a good year." "It is," Nadia said, and meant it. Then she circled the homework point, wrote 'return within a week' on next term's planner, and tucked the 'working' list into her bag to reread in August.

qa.q: How many slips went under 'to fix'?
qa.a: Four slips went under 'to fix'.

qa.q: How did Nadia feel about the year after making the two columns?
qa.a: Nadia felt genuinely satisfied and calm, because seeing twenty-six working slips beside four to fix showed that the harsh ones were only part of the picture.

qa.q: Why is Nadia's two-column rule a good habit?
qa.a: It gives praise the same attention as criticism, while still pulling out one clear change, returning homework within a week.

qa.q: How might students feel next term if homework comes back faster?
qa.a: They would likely feel that their feedback was heard and taken seriously.

grounding: Shows a young teacher deliberately counting positive feedback alongside criticism before judging the year, and still acting on the criticism.

passage: At the end of term at the Pune school, Kunal sat in the empty staff room with his class records. His first instinct was to write "a bad term." Three students had failed the unit test, a parent had complained, and his lesson on fractions had flopped. Those were the moments that kept him up at night. But he knew his mind did that, so he opened the notebook where he wrote one good thing every Friday. Twelve entries. A shy girl had spoken in class for the first time. The reading scores were up. The whole class had helped a boy with a broken arm. Maria, the head of department, had written a note after observing him: "Warm, clear, patient." Kunal made two columns, wins and setbacks, and gave them equal space. Then he wrote his review: "A mixed term, mostly good. Three things to fix."

qa.q: How many entries were in Kunal's Friday notebook?
qa.a: Twelve entries.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling before he opened his notebook?
qa.a: He felt discouraged, ready to call it a bad term because the setbacks kept him up at night.

qa.q: Which choice made Kunal's review fair?
qa.a: Reading his weekly good-things notebook and giving wins and setbacks equal space before deciding how the term went.

qa.q: How does Maria see Kunal's teaching?
qa.a: Maria sees him as warm, clear and patient, from observing his class.

grounding: Shows a grounded teacher deliberately noting good events and counting wins alongside setbacks before judging the term.

passage:
Dear Farhan,
You asked for my honest view of your first year as team lead, so here it is, and I've tried to be fair.
I know the three things you keep repeating: the delayed launch, the client who left, the bad meeting in July. They're real. But I also went through my own notes from the year before writing this, because I know how easily the bad moments crowd out the rest.
Here's the rest. Your team's attrition went to zero. Two juniors got promoted because you coached them. You fixed the testing process nobody else would touch. The client survey scored you highest in the department.
Setbacks: three. Wins: at least four, and bigger. Please weigh them the same way I have.
Warmly,
Arohi

qa.q: How many setbacks does Arohi list?
qa.a: Setbacks: three.

qa.q: What does Arohi seem to feel about Farhan's view of the year?
qa.a: Arohi seems caring and a little concerned, aware that Farhan is letting three bad moments crowd out the good ones.

qa.q: What did Arohi do before writing, and why was it fair?
qa.a: Arohi went through notes from the whole year and listed wins and setbacks side by side, so the negatives didn't outweigh the positives.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Farhan might feel surprised and relieved, seeing the overlooked wins counted as seriously as the mistakes.

grounding: A letter shows a grounded colleague deliberately counting wins alongside setbacks and giving positive feedback equal weight before judging a year.

passage: Saurabh, you asked how I stopped hating my job last year. Honestly? I'm Anand, and I used to go home and replay only the bad stuff. The angry customer. The shipment that went missing. My manager's one sharp email. After six months I was sure the job was a disaster and started drafting a resignation. Then an older colleague told me to try something for one month: every evening, write three things that went well, and three that didn't. Equal space. And to reread any good feedback as carefully as the bad. The first week, I had to think hard for the good ones. By the third week they came easily. A customer thanked me by name. My route plan saved two hours. A trainee said I explain things well. At the end of the month, the list didn't look like a disaster. It looked like a normal, decent job. I deleted the draft.

qa.q: How many things did Anand write each evening?
qa.a: Three things that went well, and three that didn't.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling after six months of replaying only the bad stuff?
qa.a: Anand felt miserable and hopeless about the job, sure it was a disaster, enough to start drafting a resignation.

qa.q: Why did the colleague's method work for Anand?
qa.a: Giving good and bad events equal space, and rereading good feedback as carefully as bad, balanced the record so Anand could judge the job fairly.

qa.q: How might the older colleague see Anand's change?
qa.a: The colleague would probably feel glad and a bit proud to see a simple habit help Anand stay.

grounding: A young worker describes deliberately noting good events and counting wins alongside setbacks, which changes the way the job looks.

passage:
I'm Nikita, and I've shared a flat with Mahima for two years, so I've watched her little ritual up close.
Every night, after brushing her teeth, she opens a thin blue notebook and writes a few lines. I peeked once when she left it on the sofa. One side of the page said: lost the client pitch; boss annoyed; missed the bus. The other side: finished the report early; new intern thanked me; mango season.
Last month, after a rough review at work, she came home looking flattened. I expected her to sulk all weekend. Instead she sat with the blue notebook and flipped back through six months of pages, counting under her breath. Then she said, mostly to herself, "Okay. Twenty-one setbacks, sixty-something good things. One bad review isn't the whole story."
I don't know exactly what she felt. But on Monday she asked her manager to put the positive feedback in writing too.

qa.q: What colour is Mahima's notebook?
qa.a: Mahima's notebook is thin and blue.

qa.q: What did Mahima seem to feel when she came home after the review?
qa.a: Mahima seemed flattened and discouraged, before the notebook helped her weigh the setbacks against the good things.

qa.q: Why was asking the manager for positive feedback in writing a good step?
qa.a: It gives good feedback the same weight and record as criticism, so Mahima can judge how things really are.

qa.q: How does Nikita experience watching the ritual?
qa.a: Nikita is curious and a little surprised, expecting a sulky weekend and instead seeing Mahima calmly count wins against setbacks.

grounding: Shows, through a flatmate's account, a young woman who records good events beside setbacks and weighs praise as much as criticism.

Monday. The client call went badly; they hated the colour scheme. Sangeeta walked out of the meeting room thinking, this whole project is a disaster. Before she could send an angry message to the team, she opened a blank page and made two columns: went wrong, went right. Went wrong: colours, one late file. Went right: layout approved, deadline met, client praised Eshaan's icons.
Wednesday. At the team review, she started with the right-hand column, reading each item out. Then the colours. Eshaan, who had been bracing for a scolding, sat up.
Friday. The redesign went to the client. Sangeeta sent Eshaan a separate note: "Your icons were the best part of Monday's call. I should have said so on Monday." He replied with a thumbs-up and three exclamation marks.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling as she left the meeting room?

passage:
Chetan, you've been staring at that one bad review since morning. Let me tell you how I nearly closed my dhaba.
I opened it on the highway outside Ambala when I was twenty-five. In the first month, a truck driver wrote on the wall in charcoal: "Worst dal in Punjab." I read that line every morning for a week. I stopped trying new dishes.
My mother's cousin, who kept the accounts, put a slate next to the till. "Every plate that comes back empty, one line. Every complaint, one cross." By the end of the month there were four crosses and more than six hundred lines.
I, Baljeet, stood looking at that slate a long time. Then I painted over the charcoal, and put the dal back on the menu with a little more ghee.
So. How many good reviews did you get this month?

qa.q: What did the truck driver write on the wall?
qa.a: The truck driver wrote, 'Worst dal in Punjab.'

qa.q: Why did Baljeet stop trying new dishes that first month?
qa.a: Baljeet felt hurt and discouraged, reading the charcoal line every morning until it seemed to be the whole truth.

qa.q: Which choice in the story turned things around, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the slate, a line for every empty plate and a cross for every complaint, showed four crosses against six hundred lines and balanced the record.

qa.q: How might the cousin who kept the accounts have seen Baljeet that week?
qa.a: The cousin probably saw a worried young owner fixed on one insult and wanted to show the plain numbers instead.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how counting good plates beside complaints gave praise as much weight as one harsh insult.

passage: Farhan had twenty minutes before the vegetable supplier's order deadline, and the café's power had just gone out, so he sat by the window with a notebook and his phone torch. That morning a one-star review had called his biryani "bland and overpriced". His first instinct was to scrap the biryani and order extra paneer instead. Farida, his partner in the café, watched him stop and draw two columns. Last month: the one-star review, two late deliveries. Also last month: forty-one good reviews, eleven of them praising the biryani, and a regular who now brought her whole office on Fridays. He read both columns twice. "One review is loud," he said. "Forty-one are quiet." He placed the usual biryani order, added a note to taste-test the spice with Farida on Monday, and sent it with two minutes to spare.

qa.q: How many of the good reviews praised the biryani?
qa.a: Eleven of the forty-one good reviews.

qa.q: How did Farhan seem to feel right after the one-star review?
qa.a: He seemed stung and anxious enough to want to scrap the biryani, before he stopped to look at the whole record.

qa.q: What did Farhan's two columns help him decide?
qa.a: Seeing the setbacks next to the forty-one good reviews showed the biryani was mostly loved, so he kept it and planned a spice taste-test.

qa.q: How might Farida see Farhan's pause?
qa.a: Farida is probably relieved and reassured to see him weigh both columns instead of reacting to one loud review.

grounding: Shows a person counting wins alongside setbacks and giving positive feedback as much weight as negative before deciding.
